intro: Frank Lévy plays a nocturne that keeps turning a solo song into a duet. A stream of left-hand semiquavers runs beneath three statements of the D♭-major melody, each with something new to say.

sections.label: A · Broken chords, then a singer
sections.mNote: The left hand begins alone; the melody enters on F

sections.label: B · Two voices in B♭ minor
sections.mNote: The right hand sings in thirds above the continuing semiquavers

sections.label: A′ · F above the D♭ bass
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns, marked dolce

sections.label: B′ · C♯ and E in the duet
sections.mNote: The paired melody turns towards A major and C♯ minor

sections.label: A″ · The song returns a third time
sections.mNote: D♭ major returns before the right hand breaks into flourishes

sections.label: Coda · D♭ beneath the changing chords
sections.mNote: The bass holds its ground while the upper notes descend

cues.title: The left hand alone
cues.text: The left hand opens the nocturne alone, spreading D♭ major across the keyboard in groups of six semiquavers. In the next bar the right hand begins on F, marked dolce. Its first phrase floats over a bass that keeps returning to D♭.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 1–4; Mutopia transcription: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A second singer
cues.text: The single melody becomes a duet in thirds. B♭ enters the bass, turning the harmony towards the relative minor. The right hand sings espressivo, while the left keeps up its long sweeps of semiquavers.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 10–13: paired right-hand notes and B♭-minor harmony. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: From Geneva to New York
cues.text: Lévy enters the Geneva Conservatory at fifteen, later studies with Maria Tipo and Leon Fleisher, and spends thirteen years teaching in Juilliard’s Pre-College Division. In 2014 he joins Musopen’s project to record Chopin’s complete works.
cues.evidence: Frank Lévy’s San José State University biography documents his studies, Juilliard post (1995–2008) and 2014 Musopen collaboration: https://www.sjsu.edu/music/faculty-staff/directory/frank-levy.php

cues.title: The opening F returns
cues.text: After the wandering harmonies, F returns above a deep D♭. The first melody starts again, a tempo and dolce. Its long notes soon gather more ornaments, including a feather-light run marked leggierissimo.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 26–33; leggierissimo at bar 32. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The duet changes spelling
cues.text: D♭ and F become C♯ and E in the right hand. The bass keeps the same sounding C♯, but an A♮ in the accompaniment changes the chord to A major. The duet has stepped into a new room without moving its floor.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 33–34: D♭-major harmony changes to A major over C♯, with C♯ and E in the right hand. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The third verse
cues.text: The opening melody comes home again over D♭. This time its continuation swells into a long written-out flourish: a stream of small notes climbs high, then tumbles back down through the right hand.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 46–52: third return and the extended ornamental figure at bars 51–52. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: D♭ holds the floor
cues.text: The bass settles on D♭ and keeps renewing it. Above, the right hand makes a descending chain of little sighs, each beginning high and falling. Chopin marks the passage dolcissimo, very sweetly.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 62–68: recurring D♭ bass, dolcissimo and descending paired figures. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Mendelssohn learns it by ear
cues.text: In September 1835 Chopin plays this nocturne at Friedrich Wieck’s house in Leipzig. Mendelssohn is there, and writes to his sister Fanny about the “lovely new notturno”, a considerable part of which he has learnt by ear.
cues.evidence: Mendelssohn’s letter to Fanny after Chopin’s September 1835 visit, quoted in John Henken’s Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note: https://www.laphil.com/works/two-nocturnes-op-27

cues.title: Sixths climb into the treble
cues.text: Two notes at a time climb in sixths through two groups of seven. The marking is dolcissimo e diminuendo: very sweetly, growing softer. The hands finally come to rest on D♭ major.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 75–77: ascending sixths in septuplets, dolcissimo e diminuendo, final D♭-major chord. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: B♭ beneath two singing voices
transitions.from: A · Broken chords, then a singer
transitions.to: B · Two voices in B♭ minor
transitions.how: The D♭-major phrase comes to rest on F. The bass moves to B♭, and the right hand adds D♭ below that F: the new phrase starts in B♭ minor, with two voices singing in thirds. The left hand keeps the same six-note sweep beneath them. Chopin marks the duet espressivo.

transitions.title: A♭ resolves to D♭
transitions.from: B · Two voices in B♭ minor
transitions.to: A′ · F above the D♭ bass
transitions.how: The bass reaches A♭, with C and G♭ making the dominant seventh of D♭. The right hand climbs towards F as that chord resolves onto a low D♭. The opening melody returns, marked a tempo and dolce; the left-hand semiquavers continue without a break.

transitions.title: F falls to E
transitions.from: A′ · F above the D♭ bass
transitions.to: B′ · C♯ and E in the duet
transitions.how: The duet’s D♭–F pair changes to C♯–E. D♭ and C♯ are the same piano key, so the bass holds its sounding pitch while F falls a semitone. A♮ enters the left-hand arpeggio, making an A-major chord over C♯. The paired melody continues above the familiar semiquavers.
transitions.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 33–34. The A-major chord over C♯ precedes the later C♯-minor passage. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486

transitions.title: A falling run finds F
transitions.from: B′ · C♯ and E in the duet
transitions.to: A″ · The song returns a third time
transitions.how: A right-hand run falls across the keyboard while the left hand reaches A♭ dominant-seventh harmony. The bass then drops to D♭, and F begins the familiar melody for the third time. Dolce replaces the forceful accents of the preceding passage.

transitions.title: The bass stays on D♭
transitions.from: A″ · The song returns a third time
transitions.to: Coda · D♭ beneath the changing chords
transitions.how: A♭ dominant harmony resolves onto D♭ in the bass. The right hand answers with a high D♭ falling to G, then continues down in similar pairs, marked dolcissimo. Each changing chord retains D♭ underneath. The left hand still moves, but its lowest note stays put.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
